<main class="s-page">

<header>
  <p class="s-title" role="heading" aria-level="1">Research</p>
  <p class="s-lede">I study what people with chronic conditions in Kenya pay for care, what insurance actually covers when they reach a clinic, and how facility finances decide whether medicines are on the shelf.</p>
  <p>Most of my recent work uses the 2022 Kenya Demographic and Health Survey, the last national survey before NHIF was replaced by the Social Health Authority in October 2024, so these estimates serve as a pre-transition baseline. Alongside it I run mixed-methods facility studies and contribute data management and survival analysis to oncology research in western Kenya.</p>
  <ul class="s-links">
    <li><a href="https://orcid.org/0009-0008-1501-601X">ORCID 0009-0008-1501-601X</a></li>
    <li><a href="thesis.html">MSc thesis</a></li>
  </ul>
</header>

<section class="s-section" aria-labelledby="themes-h">
  <h2 class="s-label" id="themes-h">Themes</h2>
  <div class="s-themes">
    <div>
      <h3>Health financing and Kenya's SHA transition</h3>
      <p>Insurance coverage, point-of-care payment and affordability barriers, measured before the switch from NHIF so later SHA data has something to be compared against.</p>
    </div>
    <div>
      <h3>Chronic disease care in primary health facilities</h3>
      <p>Hypertension and diabetes care in rural clinics: budgets, approvals, stockouts, treatment gaps and the case for testing diabetes remission locally.</p>
    </div>
    <div>
      <h3>Cancer outcomes and HIV</h3>
      <p>Survival and mortality risk for cancer patients with and without HIV at a referral hospital in western Kenya.</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<section class="s-section" aria-labelledby="articles-h">
  <h2 class="s-label" id="articles-h">Journal articles</h2>
  <ol class="s-pubs">

    <li class="s-pub">
      <p class="s-pub__title"><a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-026-26963-8">Financial determinants of effective hypertension and diabetes care in rural primary health facilities in Kisumu, Kenya: a mixed-methods study</a></p>
      <p class="s-pub__authors"><strong>Amollo NW</strong>, Ogol J, Museve E, Owenga JA, Aduda DO, Onguru D</p>
      <p class="s-pub__venue"><em>BMC Public Health</em> 26, 1275 (2026) <span class="s-tag s-tag--accent">First author</span></p>
      <details>
        <summary>Summary</summary>
        <p>Seven public primary care facilities in Seme Sub-County all prepared workplans and budgets, but none had a dedicated NCD budget line or formal financial autonomy. Spending needed county approval that usually took three to four weeks, sometimes more than two months, so facilities could not buy locally when central supplies failed, and six of the seven reported frequent medication stockouts. Chronic care depends on facility decision space, not only on how much money there is.</p>
      </details>
      <div class="s-pub__actions">
        <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-026-26963-8">Article (open access)</a>
        <a href="../posts/47-facility-decision-space-chronic-care/index.html">Plain-language essay</a>
        <a href="thesis.html">Thesis</a>
      </div>
    </li>

    <li class="s-pub">
      <p class="s-pub__title"><a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-026-03295-5">Addressing priority gaps in access and quality of NCD services in primary care settings in rural Kenya: a participatory approach to intervention development</a></p>
      <p class="s-pub__authors">Ouma OJ, Omondi D, Museve E, Akinyi I, <strong>Amollo NW</strong>, Ogutu S, Obinge E, Owenga J, Ayodo G, Bogers J, van Olmen J</p>
      <p class="s-pub__venue"><em>BMC Primary Care</em> 27, 192 (2026)</p>
      <details>
        <summary>Summary</summary>
        <p>A five-step participatory process with health workers and other stakeholders in Kisumu County to find the gaps in diabetes and hypertension care in primary facilities, then select, plan and implement interventions to close them. My role covered conceptualisation, data collection, data management, analysis and co-writing the results and discussion.</p>
      </details>
      <div class="s-pub__actions">
        <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-026-03295-5">Article</a>
        <a href="https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-6077243/v1">Preprint (2025)</a>
      </div>
    </li>

  </ol>
</section>

<section class="s-section" aria-labelledby="preprints-h">
  <h2 class="s-label" id="preprints-h">Preprints</h2>
  <ol class="s-pubs">

    <li class="s-pub">
      <p class="s-pub__title"><a href="https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.09.20.26363504">Insurance coverage, healthcare use, and outpatient payment among adults with disability in Kenya before the SHA transition: a secondary analysis of KDHS 2022</a></p>
      <p class="s-pub__authors"><strong>Amollo NW</strong>, Ogol J</p>
      <p class="s-pub__venue"><em>medRxiv</em>, September 2026 <span class="s-tag s-tag--accent">First author</span></p>
      <details>
        <summary>Summary</summary>
        <p>Of 40,197 adults in KDHS 2022, 6.7% met the Washington Group disability threshold. Adults with disability were more often uninsured, but that gap disappeared once wealth and education were accounted for. They used outpatient care and were hospitalised far more often under every adjustment, and 90.5% of outpatient users with disability paid something at their last visit, insured or not. The paper sets a pre-SHA benchmark and argues that SHA-era monitoring should measure payment at the point of care, not just enrolment.</p>
      </details>
      <div class="s-pub__actions">
        <a href="https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.09.20.26363504">medRxiv</a>
      </div>
    </li>

    <li class="s-pub">
      <p class="s-pub__title"><a href="https://doi.org/10.32388/GDWWI3">Type 2 diabetes remission in sub-Saharan Africa: why pragmatic lifestyle trials are a health system priority</a></p>
      <p class="s-pub__authors"><strong>Amollo N</strong>, Ogol J, Owenga JA</p>
      <p class="s-pub__venue"><em>Qeios</em>, September 2026 <span class="s-tag s-tag--accent">First author</span></p>
      <details>
        <summary>Summary</summary>
        <p>Trials in China, India, the USA, the UK and Qatar show that structured lifestyle programmes can prevent diabetes and, in some adults with early disease, put it into remission. No remission-focused randomised trial has been identified in sub-Saharan Africa, where patients often present younger and many cannot reliably get the medicines they are prescribed. We argue for a phased agenda: feasibility work, pragmatic trials in primary care, and room in guidelines for remission-oriented research.</p>
      </details>
      <div class="s-pub__actions">
        <a href="https://www.qeios.com/read/GDWWI3">Qeios</a>
      </div>
    </li>

    <li class="s-pub">
      <p class="s-pub__title"><a href="https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.05.14.26353157">Health insurance coverage, affordability barriers, and treatment gaps among Kenyan adults with diagnosed hypertension or diabetes before the Social Health Authority transition: a sex-stratified analysis of the 2022 Kenya Demographic and Health Survey</a></p>
      <p class="s-pub__authors"><strong>Amollo NW</strong>, Hyera HF, Ouma OJ</p>
      <p class="s-pub__venue"><em>medRxiv</em>, May 2026 <span class="s-tag s-tag--accent">First author</span></p>
      <details>
        <summary>Summary</summary>
        <p>Among 1,932 adults already diagnosed with hypertension or diabetes, 47.7% had any insurance, mostly through NHIF, and 63.8% were not taking medication for at least one diagnosed condition. Insurance was concentrated among wealthier households, while treatment gaps exceeded 60% in every wealth quintile. Insurance was not strongly linked to smaller treatment gaps, which suggests enrolment alone will not close them without deeper benefits, outpatient medicine access and clinics ready for continuous NCD care.</p>
      </details>
      <div class="s-pub__actions">
        <a href="https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.05.14.26353157">medRxiv</a>
      </div>
    </li>

  </ol>
</section>
